identification.summary: Storm-1674 is Microsoft's name for a cybercrime access broker that uses tools based on the public TeamsPhisher tool to distribute DarkGate malware over Microsoft Teams [S1][S2]. Microsoft observed Storm-1674 hand access to ransomware operators in September 2023, leading to Black Basta deployment [S1].
identification.notes: Storm-1xxx is Microsoft's designation for a developing cluster [S1]. Microsoft reported Storm-1674 using malicious installers and landing-page frameworks provided by Storm-1113, so the two clusters overlap operationally but are separate Microsoft clusters [S1]. Storm-1811 (Black Basta-linked Teams help-desk impersonation) is a separate Microsoft cluster and is not named in Microsoft's May 2024 Quick Assist report alongside Storm-1674 [S4].

attribution.sponsor: Non-state, financially motivated cybercrime access broker as described by Microsoft [S1][S2]. No state sponsor stated.
attribution.confidence: Not stated by Microsoft in the cited material; no confidence level published.
attribution.basis: Microsoft Threat Intelligence tracking and observation of Teams phishing, DarkGate delivery and ransomware handoffs [S1][S2].

objectives: Financial gain through initial access that is passed to ransomware operators, e.g. Black Basta in September 2023 [S1].

targeting.notes: Microsoft's December 2023 article does not describe a target sector [S1]. Lures impersonated OneDrive, SharePoint, an employment opportunity, Adobe products and a networking security tool [S1]. Victim organizations appear only as brand names in indicator domains [S1]. Targets are Microsoft Teams tenants reachable by external chat or meeting messages [S1][S2].

capabilities.summary: Storm-1674 used tools based on the public TeamsPhisher red-team tool to send Teams phishing lures, typically ZIP files containing an LNK file that drops DarkGate and Pikabot [S1][S2]. From December 2023 its Teams messages led to fake SharePoint/OneDrive-style landing pages; clicking a PDF showed a fake error, and clicking OK invoked the ms-appinstaller handler to install malware, likely SectopRAT or DarkGate [S1]. It used malicious installers and landing-page frameworks provided by Storm-1113 [S1]. It created tenants to make meetings and send chat messages through meeting chat, which Microsoft assesses was meant to avoid the accept/block screen shown for one-on-one and group chats [S1]. Microsoft reports no exploited CVEs; none are cited here.

campaigns.name: Handoffs to Black Basta operators
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed handoffs from Storm-1674 to ransomware operators that led to Black Basta ransomware deployment [S1].

campaigns.name: ms-appinstaller and Teams meeting-chat lures
campaigns.summary: Storm-1674 was one of several actors abusing the ms-appinstaller URI scheme to distribute malware, together with Teams phishing using tenants it created and meeting chats, fake SharePoint landing pages, and spoofed software lures. Microsoft blocked confirmed malicious tenants, added an accept/block screen for external meeting chats, and disabled ms-appinstaller by default in App Installer 1.21.3421.0 [S1].

campaigns.name: Microsoft Teams threat disruption report
campaigns.summary: Microsoft cited Storm-1674 as the access broker using TeamsPhisher to distribute DarkGate and other payloads over Teams, and published Teams hardening guidance (external-domain allow-listing, Safe Links/Attachments for Teams, Quick Assist removal) [S2].

diamond.adversary: Storm-1674, a financially motivated access broker per Microsoft; ties to Storm-1113 (tooling) and to Black Basta operators (handoff) [S1].
diamond.capability: TeamsPhisher-based Teams phishing; DarkGate, Pikabot, possibly SectopRAT; LNK-in-ZIP droppers; ms-appinstaller abuse; fake SharePoint/OneDrive pages [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Actor-created Microsoft Teams tenants used for meeting chats; lookalike domains (e.g. tech-department[.]us subdomains, kellyservices-hr[.]com, SharePoint-style subdomains); Storm-1113-provided installers and landing-page frameworks [S1].
diamond.victim: Organizations with Teams tenants permitting external messaging; sector not specified by Microsoft [S1][S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Cybercrime ecosystem role: initial access supplier to ransomware operators; no political motive stated [S1].
diamond.technology: Microsoft Teams (external chat/meeting chat), Entra ID tenants, Windows App Installer / ms-appinstaller handler, SharePoint/OneDrive brand spoofing [S1][S2].

gaps: No Microsoft statement of confidence or any government attribution found.
Target sectors and geography are not described in cited sources.

Activity after October 2025 not verified. Search summaries referenced a Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Teams post and an April 2026 Microsoft helpdesk-impersonation playbook, and a claim that Storm-1674 compromised tenants and phoned users over Teams from November 2024; none were opened or confirmed in the Microsoft October 2025 article, so none are asserted here.
The VEILdrive primary report (Hunters Team AXON) and Truesec/CyberMaxx analyses of DarkGate Teams chains could not be opened or verified; they are not used as sources.
Malpedia and MISP galaxy entries (not fetched) may list further names or references.
Hash and domain IOCs in the Microsoft appendix were not extracted. MITRE ATT&CK group ID not assigned.
Earlier-draft claims linking Storm-1674 to VEILdrive and Sangria Tempest IT-impersonation could not be verified and were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2 (environment): Teams external-federation and meeting-chat features are the exposed surface; a tenant allowing external chat from unknown tenants is key cyber terrain [S1][S2]. Step 3 (adversary): a criminal access broker whose product is initial access sold or passed to ransomware operators [S1]. Step 4 MLCOA: Teams phishing from actor-created tenants with ZIP/LNK or fake SharePoint-page lures delivering DarkGate/Pikabot, followed by ransomware-operator handoff [S1][S2]. Candidate indicators: inbound external Teams meeting-chat messages from new or trial tenants, LNK files in ZIP attachments, ms-appinstaller invocations, lookalike SharePoint domains [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share Teams-delivered DarkGate/Pikabot indicators and Microsoft tenant-block outcomes across the cyber defense chain [S1][S2]. Authorities: tenant external-access policy changes and blocking of trial-only tenants need system-owner and DAO approval before enforcement [S2]. Mission assurance: restrict external Teams chat to allow-listed domains, enable Safe Links/Attachments for Teams, remove unused Quick Assist, and apply ASR rules, since collaboration tools may be mission-essential [S1][S2]. Coordination: report suspected Teams phishing through user reporting and SecOps review, and coordinate with Microsoft for malicious-tenant takedown [S1][S2].
